name: llama_index

facts.description: LlamaIndex is the document processing platform for AI

title: LlamaIndex: Document Processing and Data Framework for AI Applications
answer: LlamaIndex is an open source Python framework, made by Run Llama, for connecting large language models to your own data. It sits in the data and orchestration layer of AI work, handling ingestion, indexing, retrieval and agent workflows, and it is best known for retrieval augmented generation. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its centre of gravity has moved toward document parsing and managed cloud services, so check which parts you need to self host.

sections.body: LlamaIndex is an open source framework written in Python and released under the MIT licence, maintained by the company Run Llama. The project repository is run-llama/llama_index, and this site records it as active rather than archived, with a last push in October 2026 and roughly fifty two thousand stars. It occupies the data layer of the AI stack, the part between raw documents and a language model. Its own description calls it the document processing platform for AI, and the official site splits into a Python framework reference and a LlamaParse product for parsing documents. In practice it is the glue that turns files, databases and APIs into something a model can query.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The framework covers the concrete jobs around language models rather than the models themselves. It ingests and splits documents, builds indexes and vector stores, retrieves context, and runs agents and chat engines. The API reference shows a central LLM class for interacting with language models, with predict, stream, structured predict and async variants, plus tool calling through a ReAct agent by default. Integrations reach many providers, including Cloudflare AI Gateway for routing across providers with fallback and load balancing, Baseten for dedicated and model API endpoints, and Vertex AI for embeddings and vector search. It is strongest where retrieval quality and document handling matter, and the GraphRAG example shows how far that goes, building entity graphs, communities and summaries over source documents.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The learning curve is moderate for basic retrieval and steeper for the advanced paths. You need working Python, and some familiarity with embeddings, vector search and prompt construction helps considerably. The GraphRAG example assumes more, since it uses graspologic, scipy and numpy for hierarchical Leiden community detection, and it requires a Google Cloud project with the Vertex AI API enabled. Mathematics is not a prerequisite for ordinary use, but graph and clustering work rewards it. The official site offers a large body of runnable notebooks and API references, which is a genuine on ramp for a beginner, though the material assumes you can read code and configure cloud credentials.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem is broad and integration led. The site documents provider specific packages such as llama-index-llms-baseten and llama-index-llms-vertex, vector store packages such as llama-index-vector-stores-vertexaivectorsearch, and embedding classes such as VertexTextEmbedding. LlamaParse adds a self hosted parsing product with centralized provider configuration, supporting gateways including Bifrost, Portkey and LiteLLM, custom endpoints and headers, multiple credentials and managed embeddings. Documentation is extensive, with API references and cookbook examples, and the repository's star count and recent activity indicate a substantial community. The site does not give forum or chat support details, so the shape of day to day community help is not settled by this material.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: It serves both ends, with different costs. Prototyping is fast because a few lines connect a model to documents, and the notebook examples are designed to be run and adapted. Production use is supported through explicit controls, including async methods, streaming, retries and timeouts, provider fallback, and per tier model ordering in self hosted parsing where models are tried in descending priority and skipped when credentials fail. The cost is configuration surface. Centralized provider configuration, gateway bindings and tier tags are powerful but demand care, and the site notes that a recognized model identifier is not a guarantee of upstream availability. Some features are also incomplete, such as binding support in the Cloudflare gateway class, which raises a not implemented error.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The facts show a widely used, actively maintained project rather than a legacy choice. Fifty two thousand stars, a recent push and an MIT licence point to current relevance, and the breadth of provider integrations suggests adoption across teams that need retrieval over private data. The site does not name specific companies or industries using it, so any claim about who deploys it in production would go beyond the evidence. For someone choosing what to learn, the practical signal is that retrieval and document processing skills transfer well, and LlamaIndex is a reasonable place to build them, while the managed LlamaParse side reflects the industry shift toward paid document infrastructure.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LlamaIndex is a Python framework, and the site's examples are Python notebooks and API references throughout. It is typically used alongside model providers rather than instead of them, with integrations for OpenAI, Azure, Vertex AI, Baseten, Cloudflare AI Gateway and HuggingFace appearing in the material. It also sits beside vector stores and embedding services, and beside gateways such as LiteLLM, Portkey and Bifrost in self hosted deployments. The polyglot pattern is a Python data and orchestration layer calling out to hosted models and stores, with the framework owning ingestion, indexing, retrieval and agent logic while the model and storage layers remain external services.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: Several limits are visible in the material. Binding support in the Cloudflare AI Gateway class is not yet implemented, and output parsing is not supported for streaming, which raises a not implemented error. In the GraphRAG example only relationship descriptions are used at retrieval time, with entity descriptions promised for a future implementation. Async operations on Baseten are not supported with model APIs endpoints and require a webhook. The official site does not state benchmark performance, pricing for the managed product, or a support policy, and it does not name production users. Questions about long term API stability and the balance between the open framework and the commercial parsing product are left open by what the site says.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
